title: ASEAN’s crisis plans end where the coastline begins
gist: ASEAN built substantial disaster institutions after the 2004 tsunami (AADMER, AHA Centre, ASEAN-ERAT), but they are poorly designed for crises that start at sea and degrade ports, shipping and communications needed for response. Eric Ang argues the gap is coordination 'plumbing' across land-sea boundaries and proposes maritime scenarios, dependency-testing exercises and relationship investment.

insights.claim: The 26 December 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami struck with little warning because the Indian Ocean then lacked a tsunami warning system, with Aceh in Indonesia and coastal Thailand among the hardest hit.
insights.speaker: Eric Ang
insights.so_what: Historical baseline for tail-risk events in a key trade region.

insights.claim: After the 2004 tsunami, ASEAN signed the ASEAN Agreement on Disaster Management and Emergency Response (AADMER) in 2005 and created the AHA Centre in 2011, alongside assessment teams, standby arrangements and exercises such as ARDEX.
insights.speaker: Eric Ang
insights.so_what: Regional disaster institutions exist but may not cover maritime cascading failures.

insights.claim: Satellites, seismic sensors, maritime surveillance and mobile communications now allow disasters to be detected far faster, so the challenge has shifted from seeing a crisis to acting before one failure cascades into another.
insights.speaker: Eric Ang
insights.so_what: Value in disaster resilience now lies in coordination and response capacity rather than detection tech alone.
insights.quote: The challenge is not whether we can see a crisis developing, but whether organisations can act before one failure cascades into another.
insights.locator: More than two decades later, satellites

insights.claim: A glacier collapse in the Nepal-China border region sent water and debris through the Bhote Koshi-Trishuli river system, destroying bridges and roads and disrupting hydropower and communications, illustrating how one hazard becomes a systems problem.
insights.speaker: Eric Ang
insights.so_what: Climate-driven hazards can knock out critical infrastructure including hydropower assets.
insights.quote: Infrastructure needed by responders was itself affected – one hazard rapidly became a systems problem.

insights.claim: A tsunami similar to 2004's could simultaneously damage ports, coastal communities and vessels at sea, disabling the infrastructure through which relief supplies would need to arrive.
insights.speaker: Eric Ang
insights.so_what: Port and shipping disruption in Southeast Asian trade corridors is a correlated tail risk for supply chains.

insights.claim: Extreme weather in a major maritime corridor could force authorities to manage onshore evacuations while handling ships seeking shelter, damaged navigation aids and threats to underwater infrastructure.
insights.speaker: Eric Ang
insights.so_what: Undersea cables and shipping lanes in Southeast Asia face weather-related disruption risk.

insights.claim: The author argues the shoreline is an administrative boundary rather than a disaster boundary, and in maritime crises no single organisation owns the problem as navies, coast guards, ports and commercial operators each hold different capacity and information.
insights.speaker: Eric Ang
insights.so_what: Commercial shipping and port operators are likely to be drawn into future regional disaster responses.
insights.quote: Commercial operators may hold capacity and information government responders do not possess.

insights.claim: Better visibility creates a second-order challenge: capability distributed across many organisations is not the same as coordinated capability, and information matters only if it reaches someone able to decide and mobilise action.
insights.speaker: Eric Ang
insights.so_what: Investment in interoperability and coordination may matter more than more sensors.
insights.quote: Capability distributed across many organisations is not the same as coordinated capability.

insights.claim: At ASEAN's Strategic Policy Dialogue on Disaster Management in Singapore in August 2026, the key message was that the region must move upstream toward anticipatory action.
insights.speaker: Eric Ang
insights.so_what: Signals regional policy direction toward pre-emptive disaster financing and planning.
insights.locator: At the ASEAN Strategic Policy Dialogue

insights.claim: Southeast Asia's crisis-management problem is often less about creating institutions than improving the 'plumbing' connecting them — the channels through which information, authority and decisions move.
insights.speaker: Eric Ang
insights.so_what: Regional resilience gains are likely to come from process and communication upgrades, not new bodies.
insights.locator: As Lowell Bautista and I argued

insights.claim: Ang proposes three shifts: give maritime scenarios an explicit place in regional disaster planning by mapping cross-domain dependencies, design exercises that test what happens when ports or communications fail, and invest in relationships as well as procedures.
insights.speaker: Eric Ang
insights.so_what: A roadmap for what improved ASEAN maritime disaster preparedness would look like.

insights.claim: Putting disaster agencies, militaries, humanitarian responders and maritime authorities in the same exercise is different from testing whether they can keep functioning when a port, communications network or transport system fails.
insights.speaker: Eric Ang
insights.so_what: Current multi-agency exercises may overstate actual regional resilience.
